newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian state to keep radicals out of mosques.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian state to keep radicals out of mosques.

text.p: The Egyptian government announced a series of measures on Wednesday to impose orthodoxy in the country's privately run mosques, the platform of choice for recruitment to Islamist opposition groups.

For years the government has tried, with mixed success, to keep radical Islamists out of the mosques by obtaining control of mosque finances and appointing prayer leaders favourable to its own interpretation of Islam.

Under the new plan, in effect an acceleration of this longstanding policy, the Ministry of Awqaf (religious endowments) will take over 30,000 non-governmental mosques over the next five years, at a steady rate of 6,000 a year.
Information Minister Safwat el-Sherif said the aim was to "protect the mosques from infiltration by people who are not qualified in religion and religious law".
He was speaking after a cabinet meeting which discussed the subjects and decided on the measures.

He said the state would spend 17 million pounds ($5 million) on appointing 6,500 qualified graduates from al-Azhar Islamic university to run the mosques. Al-Azhar, a state-run institution, is the bastion of Sunni Moslem orthodoxy.
In the meantime, all the activities of non-governmental organisations which run mosques would be subject to supervision by the Ministry of Awqaf, he added.
The state will also review the religious programmes broadcast on state radio and television, sometimes criticised by liberals as an incitement to religious extremism.

"A committee with representatives from the Ministry of Information and the Ministry of Awqaf will set guidelines for the subjects religious programmes deal with and for choosing the best speakers from among enlightened scholars who are capable of relating properly with the public," Sherif said.
Several Islamist militant groups have been fighting since the early 1990s to overthrow the Egyptian government and turn the country into a strict Islamic state.
More than 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which the Egyptian police have managed to confine mainly to about four provinces in the Nile valley south of Cairo.
The main militant organisation is the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), which has traditionally run its own mosques with their own radical preachers.
The outlawed but influential Moslem Brotherhood, which does not advocate violence, has also used mosques and private Islamic charity organisations as a vehicle for its ideas.

The government newspaper al-Ahram said that in response to the discovery of a group trying to promote Shi'ite Moslem ideas in Egypt, a government committee would also consider legislation to prevent the spread of such ideas. Police are holding 56 members of the group for questioning.
Shi'ite Islam is almost unknown in Egypt but the government has often accused Shi'ite Iran of helping Egyptian militants.
